question: In its communication of 20 January 2026 entitled ‘Union of Equality: Anti-Racism Strategy 2026-2030’ (COM(2026)0012), the Commission refers to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism as a guiding tool.

However, given that its use has been systematised to shield the State of Israel and discredit critical voices regarding the crimes committed by Israel in Gaza and the West Bank; and considering that even its original author, Kenneth Stern, has publicly criticised the use of the definition as an instrument of censorship – opposing its legislative adoption by universities and governments, noting that it limits academic freedom and freedom of expression, and warning that it has been used to threaten various institutions and figures with lawsuits and to label critics of Israeli policy as antisemitic12; and also taking into account the stance of Jewish organisations in Europe and worldwide, which question the application of the definition in contexts that conflict with free expression: Does the Commission plan to ABANDON this definition and replace it with an alternative interpretive framework, such as the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism, while also incorporating explicit safeguards to ensure full compatibility with Articles 11 and 12 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and to avoid a chilling effect, as noted by the author himself, on protest?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.4.2026)

The Commission has been using the non-legally binding working definition of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition1 since 2017 as a tool in recognising contemporary forms of antisemitism. The 2018 survey by the Fundamental Rights Agency (FRA) among Jewish Europeans shows that the examples in the definition reflect what the vast majority perceives as antisemitic2.

The Commission therefore considers the IHRA definition as the benchmark for promoting a rights-based and victim-centred approach to combating antisemitism3. Member States endorsed the use of the IHRA definition in Council Conclusions on combating racism and antisemitism, adopted on 4 March 2022.

The use of the IHRA definition is consistent with the EU Strategy on combating antisemitism and fostering Jewish life (2021-2030) and was reaffirmed by the Council in 20244. The IHRA definition does not limit freedom of expression as the examples of the definition clearly state that ‘criticism of Israel similar to that levelled against any other country cannot be regarded as antisemitic’.
Antisemitic acts are criminal when they are so defined by law.

discrimination-and-hate. 3 The drafting of the original working definition took place under the umbrella of the European Union Monitoring Centre and in an OSCE context and included a variety of experts who continue to support the definition. 4 https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-14245-2024-INIT/en/pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com.
